questions.stem: Who appoints the Governor of a state in India?

options.text: The Chief Minister of the state

questions.explanation: The Governor is appointed by the President of India (Article 155) and holds office during the pleasure of the President (Article 156). Although called an appointment by the President, it is effectively made on the advice of the central government. The Governor is the constitutional head of the state.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: What is the minimum age qualification to be appointed as a Governor?
questions.explanation: A person must have completed 35 years of age to be eligible for appointment as Governor (Article 157). The other qualifications are that the person must be a citizen of India and must not hold any office of profit. This is the same minimum age as for the President.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: What is the normal term of office of a Governor?
questions.explanation: A Governor holds office for a term of 5 years, but this is subject to the pleasure of the President (Article 156). In practice, a Governor can be removed or transferred earlier, and there is no fixed security of tenure. A Governor continues in office until a successor takes charge.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Governor is the constitutional head of the state, analogous to which office at the central level?
questions.explanation: The Governor is the constitutional (nominal) head of a state, analogous to the President at the Union level. Just as the President acts on the advice of the Union Council of Ministers, the Governor normally acts on the advice of the State Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister (Article 163).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which article of the Constitution provides for the appointment of a Governor for the states?
questions.explanation: Article 153 provides that there shall be a Governor for each state. Article 155 deals with appointment, 156 with term, 157 with qualifications, and 163 with the council of ministers aiding the Governor. Article 356 deals with President's Rule (state emergency), and Article 200 with the Governor's assent to bills.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Can one person be appointed as Governor of two or more states?

options.text: Yes, the same person can be appointed Governor of two or more states

questions.explanation: Yes — Article 153 (with a proviso added by the 7th Amendment, 1956) allows the same person to be appointed as Governor of two or more states simultaneously. This is fairly common in practice, especially for smaller or northeastern states.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: When a bill passed by the state legislature is presented to the Governor, which of the following is NOT an option available to the Governor under Article 200?

options.text: Personally amend the bill and enact it
Reserve the bill for the President's consideration

questions.explanation: Under Article 200, the Governor may: (a) give assent, (b) withhold assent, (c) return the bill (if not a money bill) for reconsideration, or (d) reserve the bill for the President. The Governor CANNOT personally amend and enact a bill — that is not a constitutional option. If the legislature passes a returned bill again, the Governor must give assent.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Governor has the power to nominate members to the State Legislative Council (where it exists) from which fields?

options.text: Literature, science, art, cooperative movement, and social service

questions.explanation: The Governor nominates members to the State Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) who have special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art, the cooperative movement, and social service (Article 171). This parallels the President's power to nominate to the Rajya Sabha. About 1/6th of the council's members are so nominated.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Governor appoints the Chief Minister of the state. Whom does the Governor appoint as CM?

options.text: The leader of the party or coalition that commands a majority in the State Legislative Assembly
Any person of the Governor's personal choice
The candidate nominated by the President

questions.explanation: By convention, the Governor appoints as Chief Minister the leader of the party or coalition that commands a majority in the Legislative Assembly. In a hung assembly, the Governor exercises discretion in inviting a leader to form the government and prove a majority. The CM and council of ministers are then collectively responsible to the Assembly.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The oath of office to the Governor is administered by:

options.text: The Chief Justice of the High Court of that state

questions.explanation: The oath of office to the Governor is administered by the Chief Justice of the High Court of that state, and in his/her absence, the senior-most judge available (Article 159). The Governor swears to preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution and to devote himself to the service and well-being of the people of the state.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Governor's power to grant pardons under Article 161 does NOT extend to:

options.text: Pardons for offences against state laws
Death sentences (which only the President can pardon) and sentences by court-martial

questions.explanation: Under Article 161, the Governor can grant pardons, reprieves, respites, and remissions for offences against laws within the state's executive power. However, unlike the President (Article 72), the Governor CANNOT pardon a death sentence, and cannot grant pardons in court-martial (military) cases. The power to pardon death sentences rests solely with the President.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which of the following officials is appointed by the Governor?

options.text: The Advocate General of the state

questions.explanation: The Governor appoints the Advocate General of the state (Article 165), the state's highest law officer. High Court judges are appointed by the President; the CEC and CAG are also appointed by the President. The Governor also appoints the State Public Service Commission chairman/members (though they can only be removed by the President).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Is the Governor entitled to any immunity from legal proceedings while in office?

options.text: Immunity from criminal proceedings and from arrest during the term of office (Article 361)
Immunity only with Supreme Court permission

questions.explanation: Under Article 361, the Governor (like the President) enjoys immunity: no criminal proceedings can be instituted against them during their term, and they cannot be arrested or imprisoned while in office. They are also not answerable to any court for the exercise of their official powers. Civil proceedings regarding personal acts require two months' notice.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: When a state is under President's Rule (Article 356), who administers the state?

options.text: The Chief Minister continues as usual
The Governor administers the state on behalf of the President, with the assistance of advisers
The Chief Justice of the High Court
The Speaker of the dissolved Assembly

questions.explanation: During President's Rule (State Emergency under Article 356), the state government is dismissed and the Governor administers the state on behalf of the President, usually with the help of advisers (often retired civil servants). The state legislature's powers are exercised by Parliament. President's Rule is initially for 6 months, extendable.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Governor submits a report to the President recommending President's Rule when:

options.text: The state government wins an election
The constitutional machinery in the state has broken down / the government cannot function as per the Constitution
A new Chief Minister is sworn in

questions.explanation: The Governor reports to the President recommending President's Rule when satisfied that the government of the state cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution — i.e., a breakdown of constitutional machinery. The S.R. Bommai case (1994) made this subject to judicial review to curb misuse. The proclamation must be approved by Parliament within 2 months.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which of the following is a discretionary power of the Governor (exercised without the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers)?

options.text: Summoning the budget session on ministerial advice
Reserving a bill for the President's consideration

questions.explanation: Reserving a bill for the President's consideration is a discretionary power the Governor may exercise. Other discretionary powers include: appointing a CM in a hung assembly, recommending President's Rule, and seeking information from the CM. Article 163 explicitly recognises that the Governor acts in his discretion in certain matters, unlike the President.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Special discretionary responsibilities are constitutionally given to the Governors of certain states regarding tribal areas. Which state is an example?
questions.explanation: Governors of certain states have special constitutional responsibilities — e.g., the Governor of Nagaland (Article 371A) regarding law and order, and Governors of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram regarding tribal areas under the Sixth Schedule. Maharashtra and Gujarat Governors have special responsibilities for development boards (Article 371). These add discretionary scope beyond ordinary states.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: To whom does the Governor address the resignation letter?
questions.explanation: The Governor addresses the resignation letter to the President of India, since the Governor is appointed by and holds office during the pleasure of the President (Article 156). This parallels the chain of accountability: just as a state minister resigns to the Governor, the Governor resigns to the President.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about the Governor's relationship with the state Council of Ministers (Article 163)?

options.text: The Governor must always act independently of the Council
The Council of Ministers is appointed by the President, not the Governor
There is a Council of Ministers headed by the CM to aid and advise the Governor, except where the Governor acts in his discretion
The Governor has no Council of Ministers

questions.explanation: Article 163 provides that there shall be a Council of Ministers, headed by the Chief Minister, to aid and advise the Governor in the exercise of his functions — EXCEPT where the Governor is required to act in his discretion. So the Governor is normally bound by ministerial advice, but retains a limited sphere of discretion (unlike the President, whose discretion is more constrained post-42nd/44th Amendments).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The salary and allowances of the Governor are charged on:

options.text: The Consolidated Fund of the State

questions.explanation: The salary and allowances of the Governor are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State (and are non-votable). When the same person is Governor of two or more states, the emoluments are shared among the states as the President determines. The Governor's emoluments cannot be reduced during the term of office.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: A Governor reserves a bill for the President under Article 200. If the President returns it for reconsideration and the state legislature passes it again, is the President bound to assent?

options.text: No — the Constitution does not bind the President to give assent even after reconsideration; the President may still withhold assent
Yes, the President must assent the second time, like the Governor
The bill automatically becomes law without the President
The Supreme Court decides whether it becomes law

questions.explanation: Unlike the Governor (who MUST assent if the legislature re-passes a returned bill), the President is NOT constitutionally bound to give assent to a reserved bill even after the state legislature reconsiders and re-passes it (Article 201). The President may still withhold assent, and no time limit is prescribed — which is why reserved bills can remain pending indefinitely (a recurring centre–state friction point).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which landmark case laid down guidelines restricting the arbitrary use of Article 356 (President's Rule), thereby affecting the Governor's reporting role?

options.text: S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)

questions.explanation: S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) is the landmark case where the Supreme Court laid down that the proclamation of President's Rule under Article 356 is subject to judicial review, that the floor of the Assembly is the proper place to test majority (not the Governor's subjective assessment), and that the power must not be misused. This curbed the politically motivated dismissal of state governments.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which commission/committee specifically examined Centre–State relations and made recommendations on the role and appointment of Governors?
questions.explanation: The Sarkaria Commission (1983–88) examined Centre–State relations and made key recommendations on Governors: they should be eminent persons from outside the state, not active in politics recently, appointed in consultation with the Chief Minister, and should normally complete their 5-year term. The Punchhi Commission (2007) later revisited these issues. The Kothari Commission dealt with education; Mandal with reservations.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: A Governor's 'pocket veto'-like situation arises in the Indian context when:

options.text: The Governor signs every bill immediately
The Governor vetoes a money bill
The Governor neither assents to, returns, nor reserves a bill, simply keeping it pending indefinitely as the Constitution prescribes no time limit for action

questions.explanation: Article 200 prescribes no explicit time limit for the Governor to act on a bill, so a Governor can effectively keep a bill pending indefinitely without assenting, returning, or reserving it — a 'pocket veto'-like delay. This has caused recent Centre–State disputes (e.g., Tamil Nadu, Punjab), with the Supreme Court urging Governors to act within a reasonable time, since indefinite inaction frustrates the legislature's will.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which statement about the Governor's removal is correct?

options.text: A Governor can be removed only through impeachment by Parliament, like the President
A Governor can be removed only by the state legislature
A Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President and can be removed by the President at any time; there is no fixed security of tenure or impeachment process
A Governor cannot be removed before 5 years under any circumstances

questions.explanation: A Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President (Article 156) and can be removed by the President at any time — there is no impeachment process and no fixed security of tenure (unlike the President, who can only be removed by impeachment). However, the Supreme Court (in B.P. Singhal v. Union of India, 2010) held that the removal cannot be arbitrary, capricious, or based solely on a change of government at the Centre.
questions.subject: Polity
